extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (or advanced undergraduates) studying scheme-theoretic algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, constructions, and key properties of the Segre embedding, normalization of schemes, and separated/quasi-separated morphisms; includes examples, exercises, and key theorems (finiteness of integral closure, behavior under base change and composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Segre morphism / Segre embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: The map P^m_A ×_A P^n_A → P^{mn+m+n}_A given in coordinates by ([x_0,...,x_m],[y_0,...,y_n]) ↦ [z_{ij}] with z_{ij} = x_i y_j; called the Segre morphism. If A is a field the image is the Segre variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a well-defined morphism of schemes; it is a closed embedding (the Segre embedding). Scheme-theoretically the image is cut out by the vanishing of all 2×2 minors (rank-one condition). Example: m=n=1 gives P^1 × P^1 → P^3 whose image is the quadric surface cut out by a00a11 − a01a10 = 0. Exercises and hints: 9.6.A show maps glue; 9.6.B shows the 2×2 minors generate the ideal; coordinate-free description as P(V)×P(W) → P(V⊗W) appears in 9.6.C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate-free Segre description
rubrics_metrics.description: Segre embedding interpreted as P(V) × P(W) → P(V ⊗ W) (coordinate-free).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is an associated surjective map of graded rings Sym•(V∨ ⊕ W∨) → ⊕_n (Sym^n V∨ ⊗ Sym^n W∨) (exercise 9.6.C). See also the more general description in 9.6.D for Proj of graded rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of normalization (of a reduced scheme)
rubrics_metrics.description: A normalization of a reduced scheme X is a morphism ν: X̃ → X from a normal scheme X̃ such that ν induces a bijection on irreducible components, is birational on each irreducible component, and satisfies the universal property making it unique up to unique isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For irreducible (integral) affine X = Spec A, the normalization is Spec of the integral closure of A in its fraction field K(A). Exercises (9.7.A, 9.7.B, 9.7.C) guide checking the universal property and surjectivity (Lying Over). Examples: normalization of the nodal cubic, cusp y^2 = x^3, and tacnode y^2 = x^4. Remarks: normalization resolves singularities in dimension one (under reasonable Noetherian hypotheses) but need not in higher dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization in a function-field extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an integral scheme X with function field K(X) and an algebraic field extension L/K(X), the normalization of X in L is a dominant morphism ν: X̃ → X from a normal integral scheme X̃ with function field L, universal with respect to that property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.7.I: show existence in the finite extension case. Examples: arithmetic (Spec Z in Q(i)) and geometric normalizations show interesting behavior. Use integral closure constructions in affine charts and glue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization properties: integrality, surjectivity, birationality, finiteness in finite-type cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Normalizations are integral and surjective; for integral finite-type k-schemes the normalization morphism is finite and birational; normalization is an isomorphism on an open dense subset for integral finite-type k-schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 9.7.C, 9.7.M(a,b), 9.7.N, 9.7.O guide these verifications. Strategy: check affine case using integral closure; use finite-generation/finiteness results and Noether normalization for finite morphism assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of integral closure (Theorem 9.7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A be a Noetherian integral domain with fraction field K and L/K a finite extension; let B be the integral closure of A in L. (a) If A is integrally closed and L/K is separable then B is a finitely generated A-module. (b) If A is a finitely generated k-algebra then B is a finitely generated A-module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch: reduce to Galois case and use linear algebra (matrix with σ_i(b_j) entries) to get integrality and finiteness in separable case; use Noether normalization for (b). Warning (9.7.4): integral closure of a Noetherian ring need not be Noetherian in general — examples exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of separated morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π: X → Y is separated if the diagonal morphism δ_π: X → X ×_Y X is a closed embedding. An A-scheme X is separated over A if its structure morphism X → Spec A is separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric intuition: analogue of Hausdorff condition (diagonal closed subset). Proposition 10.1.3: δ is always a locally closed embedding. Equivalent condition: the image of the diagonal is a closed subset of X ×_Y X. Exercises: verify affine morphisms are separated (10.1.C); open and closed embeddings are separated (10.1.B). Example: P^n_A → Spec A is separated (Proposition 10.1.5), with two proofs given (direct coordinate calculation and via Veronese+Segre). Non-example: the line with doubled origin is not separated (Exercise 10.1.D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of quasi-separated morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π: X → Y is quasi-separated if the diagonal morphism δ_π: X → X ×_Y X is quasi-compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent (for affine target Spec A): for two affine opens U,V ⊂ X mapping to Spec A, U ∩ V is a finite union of affine opens (exercise 10.1.G). Separated morphisms are quasi-separated. Locally Noetherian sources are automatically quasi-separated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety over a field k (important definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A k-variety is a reduced, separated scheme of finite type over k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: some sources add irreducibility; sometimes k is assumed algebraically closed. Reduced finite-type affine k-schemes are examples. Subvarieties are reduced locally closed subschemes. Morphisms of k-varieties are automatically finite type and separated (see exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separatedness and quasi-separatedness: stability under base change
rubrics_metrics.description: Both separatedness and quasi-separatedness are preserved by base change: if Y → Z has the property and W → Z is any morphism, then the base-changed morphism W ×_Z Y → W has the property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses that the diagonal's property is preserved by base change; closed embeddings and quasi-compactness are preserved by base change (Proposition 10.1.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separatedness and quasi-separatedness: local on the target
rubrics_metrics.description: Being separated (resp. quasi-separated) is local on the target: π: X → Y is separated iff for some open cover {U_i} of Y each π^{-1}(U_i) → U_i is separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use base-change preservation and the fibered-product description to reduce to checking on an open cover (Proposition 10.1.11). Similar statement/exercise (10.1.I) for quasi-separatedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separatedness and quasi-separatedness: closed under composition
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y and ρ: Y → Z are separated (resp. quasi-separated) then their composition ρ ◦ π: X → Z is separated (resp. quasi-separated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the magic diagram and that closed embeddings (resp. quasi-compact maps) are preserved under base change and composition (Proposition 10.1.13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection of affine opens in separated schemes is affine
rubrics_metrics.description: If X → Spec A is separated and U and V are affine open subsets of X, then U ∩ V is affine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: use Small Proposition 10.1.6 and that Δ is a closed subscheme of the affine U ×_A V, hence U ∩ V ≅ Δ ∩ (U ×_A V) is affine (Proposition 10.1.8). Note: this property does not characterize separatedness (counterexample: line with doubled origin over a point still has this property).

rubrics_metrics.name: Small Proposition (10.1.6): diagonal and open subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: If U and V are open subsets of an A-scheme X then Δ(U ×_A V) ≅ U ∩ V (i.e., the diagonal restricted to U ×_A V identifies with U ∩ V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural isomorphism coming from the fibered-product constructions; useful in proofs about affineness of intersections and behavior of the diagonal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective and quasi-projective schemes are separated
rubrics_metrics.description: The structural morphism P^n_A → Spec A is separated; consequently, every quasi-projective A-scheme is separated over A, and every reduced quasi-projective k-scheme is a k-variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 10.1.5 gives two proofs for P^n_A: direct calculation covering P^n × P^n by Ui×Uj and showing the diagonal is closed, or factor δ as Veronese followed by Segre and a linear map (all closed embeddings). Use composition stability to extend to quasi-projective schemes (Corollary 10.1.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph morphism properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For π: X → Y (morphism of Z-schemes) the graph Γ_π = (id, π): X → X ×_Z Y is always a locally closed embedding; if Y is separated over Z then Γ_π is a closed embedding; if Y is quasi-separated over Z then Γ_π is quasi-compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses base change of the diagonal (diagram 10.1.18.1). This is a standard method to promote diagonal properties to graph properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancellation Theorem for a property P of morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is a class of morphisms preserved by base change and composition, and X → Z is in P and the diagonal δ_ρ: Y → Y ×_Z Y is in P (for ρ: Y → Z), then in a commuting diagram X → Z ← Y with X → Y over Z, the induced map π: X ×_Z Y → Y is in P. Special cases: (i) if local closed embeddings are in P and τ is in P then π is in P; (ii) if closed embeddings are in P and τ is in P and ρ is separated then π is in P; (iii) same with quasi-compact and quasi-separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ubiquitous structural lemma lets one 'cancel' a factor when checking many properties (finite, finite type, closed embeddings, affine, quasi-compact, etc.). Diagrammatic argument summarized in section 10.1.19.
